newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Lahore voters seem unmoved by election campaign.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Lahore voters seem unmoved by election campaign.

text.p: Pakistanis go to the polls on February 3, but election fever seems strangely absent in the clogged and dusty streets of Lahore, as elsewhere.

In contrast to previous elections, the mood is sombre and campaigning is dull in Lahore, home to Nawaz Sharif, leader of the Pakistan Muslim League (PML), and charismatic ex-cricketer Imran Khan, a political newcomer.
President Farooq Leghari ordered national and provincial assembly polls after he sacked Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old government on November 5, alleging corruption and misrule.
"The people are unmoved by the speeches and are staying away from the hustings because of the degeneration of the whole process," the English-language daily The News said this week.
"They have seen these faces before. They have heard these promises before. They have been short-changed before."
Imran, a fresh face, has focused national attention on corruption, but few people in Lahore would bet on him winning a seat in either of the two constituencies he is contesting here.

Disenchantment with established politicians should help Imran, who built a cancer hospital in Lahore after ending his cricket career by leading Pakistan to victory in the 1992 World Cup. He formed his Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) last year.

"People want a change, they want to get rid of the two big parties," said Shahnaz Leghari, an airline pilot and organiser of the women's wing of Imran's party. "They want a new man, a new revolution, a new change in their life."
However, even she seemed unsure whether Imran could win a seat in Lahore. "According to the campaign, he has chances, but losing or winning is in the hands of God," she added.
Political analyst Aziz Siddiqui said Imran had injected a new element into Pakistani politics that was more important than the meagre tally of seats his party might gain at the polls.
"He lacks experience, his party lacks experience and he has an enormous deal to learn. Politically he is still very naive," Siddiqui said. "He won't get even (the seats) he is expecting.
"Electorally he may not have any impact, but he has made an impact on the political scene. Major parties are obliged to take notice of him and respond to the issues he is raising," he said.
Sharif's party seems poised to do well in Lahore, the capital of Punjab, Pakistan's most populous province.

"There is no competition against Nawaz Sharif in this constituency," boasted PML activist Ghulam Mustafa, referring to the central Lahore district won by his leader in three consecutive National Assembly (lower house) elections.

"We have heard that Imran Khan is also a candidate but he is hardly seen around, nor are his supporters or his workers," said a street vendor named Shahzad (one name). "There is no match for Mian Sahib (Sharif) in this area. This is his home seat."
Activists of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) are equally sure their candidate, Hafiz Ghulam Mohiuddin, will win.
"Inshallah (God willing), this seat will be won by Mohiuddin," said Ejaz Butt a die-hard PPP party worker said as he hoisted a tri-coloured PPP flag over an election office.
"He visits people day and night. He goes to every house, every street," Butt said. "Nawaz Sharif is not doing that."
The party workers may be going through the motions, but there is no disguising the absence of election fervour.
Pervaiz Saeed, a PPP supporter, said the campaign lacked life because of uncertainty in the PPP over whether the Supreme Court would overturn Bhutto's ouster and restore her government.
"Election fever can only come when the PPP comes into the campaign," he said. "The PPP is waiting for the Supreme Court decision and until then there is a great deal of confusion."
Some say people are preoccupied with the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan. Others point to the caretaker government's cost-cutting ban on election banners and posters.
"This has taken away election fever because a campaign is made on banners and posters. This time there is nothing, so there does not seem to be any excitement," Mustafa said.
But even he conceded that the apathy might have deeper roots in Pakistan's political malaise. "These elections are subdued because people are fed up with politicians," he said.
